job.style: a short story with Indian characters in everyday life

passage: Rohan and Priya sat in their small village shop, discussing their future. Rohan argued that moving to the city for a high-paying job was the only way to achieve development, as money could buy any comfort. Priya disagreed, pointing out that their village had a high literacy rate, defined as the proportion of the literate population in the 7 and above age group, which gave them better life skills than just earning cash. She noted that while their neighbor, Mr. Sharma, earned a massive salary, his family suffered from poor health and lack of clean water. Priya explained that development is a complex mix of goals, including health, education, and a clean environment, not just income. They looked at the national data, which showed a high per capita income for their state. Rohan assumed this meant everyone was wealthy, but Priya corrected him, explaining that averages often hide massive inequalities where a few rich people skew the figures. She emphasized that true progress requires sustainable resource use so that future generations can also thrive. They realized that while money is important, it is merely one tool among many, and a country's success is measured by how well its citizens live, learn, and stay healthy, rather than just the size of their bank accounts.

items.evidence: She noted that while their neighbor, Mr. Sharma, earned a massive salary, his family suffered from poor health and lack of clean water.
items.q: What does Mr. Sharma's family show about earning a big salary?
options: A big salary cannot ensure health and clean water
A big salary always brings health and clean water
A big salary is all that development needs
A big salary makes the whole village rich
items.explain: Mr. Sharma earned a lot, yet his family had poor health and no clean water.

wrong.why: thinks high income must bring good health
thinks development is only about money
thinks one rich person makes everyone rich

items.evidence: Priya disagreed, pointing out that their village had a high literacy rate, defined as the proportion of the literate population in the 7 and above age group, which gave them better life skills than just earning cash.
items.q: What does the literacy rate of Priya's village actually measure?
options: The literate share of those aged seven plus
The share who can write their own name
The literate share of everyone, even infants
The total number of literate adults nationwide
items.explain: Literacy rate is the proportion of literate people in the 7 and above age group.

wrong.why: thinks literacy means writing one's name
ignores the 7 and above age group
confuses a proportion with a total count

items.evidence: Rohan assumed this meant everyone was wealthy, but Priya corrected him, explaining that averages often hide massive inequalities where a few rich people skew the figures.
items.q: The state has a high per capita income. What does this figure tell us about its people?
options: The average is high, but many may be poor
Every family in the state is wealthy
Most people earn close to the average
People there must have good health too
items.explain: Averages can hide big inequalities, since a few rich people can pull the figure up.

wrong.why: thinks high per capita income means all are rich
thinks everyone earns near the average
thinks high income guarantees good health

items.evidence: She emphasized that true progress requires sustainable resource use so that future generations can also thrive.
items.q: Why does Priya say resources must be used sustainably for true progress?
options: So people in the future can also do well
So people today can earn more money
So the city can offer high-paying jobs
So the state's average income looks higher
items.explain: Sustainable use of resources lets future generations also thrive, not just people today.

wrong.why: thinks progress is only about earning more
picks Rohan's nearby idea about city jobs
links progress to the average income figure

items.evidence: They realized that while money is important, it is merely one tool among many, and a country's success is measured by how well its citizens live, learn, and stay healthy, rather than just the size of their bank accounts.
items.q: Two countries have equal income. How should we judge which one is doing better?
options: By its people's health, schooling and living standards
By the size of its people's bank savings
By which one has the larger population
By its total income and wealth only
items.explain: Success is measured by how well citizens live, learn and stay healthy, not bank balances.

wrong.why: thinks development is only about money
thinks a bigger population means doing better
thinks progress is judged only by income and wealth
